transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-03 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood CSM), Mark Rivers (Nova Eng Lead), Sofia Delgado (Nova Product), Lisa Nguyen (Nova Data Infra)
---
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick agenda: we wanted to go over the prompt sampling run we kicked off, dig into the TTFT tail behavior, and then Priya will walk through kernel-path options and a hedging suggestion. Anything to add?
[00:18] Mark Rivers: No, that's good. We mostly want to understand why we're seeing those spikes at 200–500ms and whether it's predictable from sequence length.
[00:25] Sofia Delgado: And we want to confirm what changes are safe for our compliance checks — we can't have a rollout that changes token retention.
[00:33] Jordan Li: I'll note that — also quick FYI we'll attach the security packet after this call.
[00:40] Priya Kapoor: Cool, I'll start with a quick recap of the sampling run. We pulled 1,000 anonymized prompts from the staging mirror, stratified by endpoint and by distribution of seq lengths. The run captured TTFT, first-chunk streaming latency, and kernel selection logs. The key finding: median TTFT is still ~38ms, 95th climbs to ~310ms, and we see a correlation with variable initial chunk sizes — smaller first-chunk forces different kernel paths in our runtime.
[01:15] Mark Rivers: Hmm, that 95th is higher than we expected. Did you correlate with cache warm state?
[01:20] Priya Kapoor: Yes — partially. When the KV cache was cold we saw a higher incidence of the slower kernel path, but even with warmed cache some prompts still took the slower path because of the attention pattern and the initial sequence length estimate.
[01:32] Lisa Nguyen: Is that because of the seqlen bias in our sampling? Our prod seqlen has a heavy tail due to some large user transcripts.
[01:38] Priya Kapoor: Exactly. The runtime chooses kernels based on predicted sequence length and observed window; if the predictor underestimates, we end up switching mid-stream and incur rebuffer costs.
[01:48] Alex Chen: Can you explain the 'switch mid-stream' case a bit? Is that the kernel recompile or a fallback?
[01:52] Priya Kapoor: Not recompilation in the JIT sense — it's more like selecting a different execution kernel optimized for longer sequences. We have two optimized code paths: the narrow-window fastpath and the wide-window throughput path. Switching from narrow to wide causes an extra roundtrip inside the runtime while we rebuild some KV pointers — it's an implementation quirk.
[02:10] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[02:15] Sofia Delgado: So what are the mitigation levers? Quantization? Batching?
[02:20] Priya Kapoor: We can do several things: 1) change the chunking strategy so the first chunk is slightly larger (trades initial latency vs later throughput), 2) bias the kernel selector towards the narrow-window fastpath for endpoints where seqlen distribution is < X, 3) apply hedging — we can speculatively start a lightweight wide-path and cancel if unnecessary (this costs GPU cycles), 4) prefix caching for repeated prefixes.
[02:42] Mark Rivers: Hedging sounds promising but costy. We need numbers.
[02:45] Alex Chen: Right — and Nova's cost sensitivity was flagged in the RFP. Jordan, do we have the buy-in to run a cost/latency delta analysis?
[02:52] Jordan Li: Yes we'll run a quick estimate and include a delta for burst GPU usage.
[02:57] Priya Kapoor: On the kernel choices — we tested 3 kernel polices in the sample: bias-narrow, bias-wide, and adaptive-hold. Bias-narrow reduced 95th TTFT by ~40ms on endpoints dominated by short prompts but increased median tokens-per-second by ~6% (so small throughput regression). Bias-wide lowered variability for long sequences but raised median TTFT by ~12ms. Adaptive-hold (our current) has best overall CPU/GPU utilization but the worse tail for Nova's mixed workload.
[03:35] Lisa Nguyen: That matches our telemetry — mixed workload is hard; we have a lot of short chat messages mixed with occasional long transcripts.
[03:42] Priya Kapoor: Also we observed streaming handshake delays — in some cases first-byte for streaming arrives earlier but the next chunk is delayed, causing perceived stutter. That's usually network or chunking alignment. We can tune the streaming handshake jitter buffer and reduce chunk size variance.
[04:00] Mark Rivers: Are those jitter buffer tweaks safe for our security posture? Anything touches the signed token?
[04:05] Alex Chen: It shouldn't. The streaming jitter buffer is internal to our runtime and doesn't change request-level auth. We'll document the config change.
[04:12] Sofia Delgado: Can you outline a quick experiment matrix? Like which knobs to flip first?
[04:16] Priya Kapoor: Recommended short experiment: A/B test bias-narrow vs adaptive-hold on a 10% sample of traffic for 48 hours; run the microburst stress test on staging with 1k prompts (we'll instrument TTFT microsecond traces); and produce a kernel-recommendation doc with clear tradeoffs.
[04:35] Mark Rivers: For the A/B sample, we need to ensure GDPR-safe logging — only aggregate stats.
[04:40] Jordan Li: We'll restrict logs and provide aggregated histograms; we'll also use hashing to sample without sending PII.
[04:45] Speaker 2: (background noise)
[04:50] Priya Kapoor: Quick note — we found three outlier prompts that triggered expensive attention patterns; we added them to a flag list. If Nova can provide top 50 heavy prompts, we can build special-cased short-circuits or prefix caching to avoid worst-case paths.
[05:08] Mark Rivers: We'll do that. We have a handful of known long-form transcripts from returns/complaints flow.
[05:15] Sofia Delgado: How quickly can Redwood produce the kernel-recommendation doc? We need it for our infra sync on Monday.
[05:20] Priya Kapoor: We can have a 1–2 page recommendation in 3 business days if we get the prompt sample today. The deeper kernel handoff will take another week.
[05:28] Alex Chen: Good. On security/compliance, Alex to share KMS notes — Nova asked about envelope encryption and audit logs.
[05:34] Jordan Li: We'll attach the SOC2 and our audit-log retention policies; if they need extra retention we can talk enterprise add-on.
[05:40] Lisa Nguyen: One more infra question — If we tilt to bias-narrow, does that affect caching behavior for multi-tenant pools? We need isolation guarantees.
[05:48] Priya Kapoor: Biasing selector is a per-route config; for Dedicated pools it won't cross tenants. For Hosted shared pools we can do per-customer route overrides once whitelisted.
[05:58] Mark Rivers: All right, let's talk numbers — can you read the median/95th from the sample again?
[06:03] Priya Kapoor: Median TTFT ~38ms, 90th at ~120ms, 95th at ~310ms. Bias-narrow brought 95th to ~270ms for short-heavy endpoints, adaptive-hold stayed ~310ms, bias-wide dropped variance on long sequences to ~220ms but pushed median to ~50ms.
[06:25] Sofia Delgado: For user-facing latency, median matters for UX but 95th for SLAs. We're tracking both.
[06:30] Mark Rivers: Can we create an SLO mapping doc? Like median under 50ms for chat, 95th under 350ms for mixed endpoints.
[06:36] Alex Chen: Yes, we can propose SLO targets in the recommendation doc.
[06:39] Priya Kapoor: About the streaming side: if we slightly increase the first chunk to 32 tokens for certain routes, we can bias kernel toward the fastpath and reduce mid-stream switching. Tradeoff: first-token bytes increases a bit. In our tests that raised median TTFT by ~5ms but 95th improved ~35ms.
[06:59] Lisa Nguyen: That seems like a good trade for interactive chat. For batch classification it's less important.
[07:05] Mark Rivers: Are there any runtime upgrades coming that would address the mid-stream switch cost?
[07:10] Priya Kapoor: Long-term we plan a less disruptive kernel handover that avoids rebuffer by preallocating KV pointers; that's a Q2 runtime project but not ready for pilot. For now we have config levers.
[07:22] Alex Chen: Let's open it up — any questions from Nova team?
[07:26] Sofia Delgado: Yes — curious about hedging costs: what's the expected GPU cost increase for speculative wide-path?
[07:32] Priya Kapoor: Ballpark: speculative hedging on 10% of traffic can cost 2–6% additional GPU compute depending on sequence-length distribution. We'll provide a more precise delta after the microburst run.
[07:44] Mark Rivers: For the microburst run, can you simulate our peak concurrency pattern? We have spikes up to 600 reqs/s for short messages for like 30s bursts.
[07:53] Priya Kapoor: Yes we can parameterize the staging runner to mimic 600 rps bursts. We'll include the sequence length mix.
[07:59] Alex Chen: Great. Also, small ask — can Redwood instrument first-byte and first-chunk separately in the traces? That will help us attribute the cost to network vs runtime.
[08:06] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we have instrumentation for first-byte, first-chunk, and internal kernel-switch events. We'll include trace excerpts.
[08:14] Speaker 1: (keyboard)
[08:18] Sofia Delgado: On compliance again — if we do per-route overrides on hosted, are we adding a management burden?
[08:23] Jordan Li: We'll template the per-route configs in the console and provide automation via our API to reduce ops friction.
[08:31] Mark Rivers: One more: can we get a simple heatmap of seqlen vs TTFT from the sample? That will help product prioritize prompt rewriting.
[08:38] Priya Kapoor: We'll add that to the microburst report.
[08:41] Alex Chen: Ok moving on — kernel handoff logistics. Priya, what should the Nova infra team expect?
[08:47] Priya Kapoor: Expect a session where we go through runtime logs, a short walk-through of kernel internals (high-level), and then 1hr of live profiling with Nova's sample prompts. We should have one or two Redwood runtime engineers in that handoff.
[09:01] Lisa Nguyen: Please include an ops checklist for Dedicated vs Hosted differences.
[09:06] Priya Kapoor: Will do.
[09:08] Speaker 3: (crosstalk)
[09:12] Mark Rivers: Anything else on telemetry? We want aggregated tail histograms every 15 minutes.
[09:18] Jordan Li: We can push aggregated hour and 15-minute histograms to your Datadog account; we'll coordinate via infra.
[09:24] Sofia Delgado: Are there any blockers from Redwood side to run the microburst test?
[09:28] Priya Kapoor: No blockers; just need the prompt sample and a staging token.
[09:32] Alex Chen: We'll generate a scoped staging token after the call.
[09:36] Mark Rivers: Good. Quick nit — in the sample you saw 3 prompts that triggered quadratic-ish attention blowup. Can you share obfuscated examples?
[09:43] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we'll include redacted examples; they're in the report.
[09:46] Lisa Nguyen: For the prompt sample we'll mask PII and remove user IDs.
[09:50] Sofia Delgado: Anything else on the triage plan?
[09:52] Priya Kapoor: No, that's the core of it. Minor note: we recommend a short-lived roll-out of bias-narrow to 10% to validate SLO improvement before any broader rollouts.
[10:03] Alex Chen: Ok let's summarize.
[10:05] Alex Chen: Action items: Priya will run microburst and produce kernel rec doc; Mark will share prompt set; Alex will send KMS/security note; Jordan will schedule the kernel handoff. Next call? Same time next week or earlier for the handoff.
[10:20] Mark Rivers: Let's plan handoff week of 2027-03-14; weekly sync stays for status.
[10:26] Sofia Delgado: Thanks team.
[10:29] Alex Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with links: microburst runner config (link: https://redwood.app/drive/microburst-runner), security packet (link: https://redwood.app/security/packet), kernel-recommendation draft (will be attached).
[10:44] Jordan Li: Closing notes — we'll redact logs and keep only aggregates for GDPR.
[10:49] Speaker 2: (goodbye)
[10:52] Alex Chen: Thanks all, bye.
